messages.subject: [OT] examples of good and bad graphic practice
messages.subject_clean: [OT] examples of good and bad graphic practice
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm compiling examples for a talk on producing scientific graphs in physics and chemistry. I will present 'the good, the bad, and the ugly' as a means of introduction to best practices and mistakes to avoid when making a plot, regardless of the tool being used. Maybe I'll have a few slides with the original bad graph, and a proposed improvement next to it. Of course being a ggplot2 user, I only have vague memories of truly bad and ugly graphics. Would you have a link to share presenting such examples, along the lines of Tufte's books but online?

Things that come to mind in no particular order,

- 3D pie chart
- some 2D pie charts
- 3D barplots
- double-axis
- misleading axes, and scales
- inappropriate colours
- ugly fonts
- useless "decorations" such as shadows, background image, etc.
- uninformative legend
- plot with too much information (wrong type of plot)
- export in lossy jpeg format
- manual tweaking of data points / scales

Cheers, and a Happy New Year!

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Using the code and data (reproducible example) shown below, I have drawn two maps - qplot and ggplot.
Acknowledgement: Hadley Wicham for the qplot example in ggplot2 (pages 78-79).

The issues are as follows:

1) Alaska and Hawaii are not displayed in the map. I am not sure whether the longitude and latitude data for these two States are extracted.
2) There appear to be some problems in the map created by the ggplot () - some tweaking of the code is needed.
3) I could not figure out how to add the State code to the map in qplot as well as ggplot.

I would appreciate receiving any advice/help toward resolving the issues.

Happy New Year!

Thanks and regards,

Pradip Muhuri

messages.subject: Re: forest plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Sun, Dec 30, 2012 at 7:28 PM, sania <sans...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I am using the this code to make forest plots, I want to make a change that
> is regarding geom_point(), I want to give different size to each point based
> on separate number for each point i.e. number of obsearvations, pls. help.

Use the size aesthetic in geom_point(). You didn't provide an example
with data, but here is a Q & D version that illustrates the idea:

DF <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, n = sample(50, 10))
require(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(aes(size = n))

Observe that a doubling of n results in a fourfold increase in the
area of the dot. A better way is to use scale_size_area() [in the
current version 0.9.3] or scale_area() [in previous versions]:

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(aes(size = n)) + scale_size_area()

The documentation hasn't caught up yet, but if you try scale_area() in
the current version, you'll get a warning that scale_area is
deprecated.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sania,

Here is the code for a reproducible example on forest plot, which I (as a beginner ggplot user) had written in the past with some input from Dennis.  Thanks to him.

Please ignore if this does not serve your purpose.

Thnaks,

Pradip Muhuri
#####
setwd ('E:/')
library(ggplot2)
dat <- read.table (text="
a18_34,s,     3.53, 2.31, 5.39
a18_34,sd,   3.39, 2.19, 5.25
a18_34,sdc,   2.78, 1.76, 4.38
a18_34,sdcsb, 2.52, 1.6, 3.99
a35_54,s,     2.96, 2.51, 3.49
a35_54,sd,   2.53, 2.15, 2.99
a35_54,sdc,   1.6, 1.33, 1.92
a35_54,sdcsb, 1.38, 1.14, 1.66
a55p,s,       1.84, 1.68, 2.02
a55p,sd,     1.65, 1.49, 1.81
a55p,sdc,     1.35, 1.23, 1.49
a55p,sdcsb,   1.31, 1.19, 1.45",
sep=",",
col.names=c('age', 'Model', 'Est','LCI','UCI'),
colClasses=c('character', 'character', 'numeric', 'numeric','numeric'))

  #chracter to factor
  dat$age <- factor(dat$age, levels=c ('a18_34','a35_54', 'a55p'),
                     labels=c('18-34', '35-54', '55 or Older'))

  dat$Model <- factor(dat$Model,levels=c('s', 'sd','sdc', 'sdcsb'),
                        labels=c('SPD Only',
                                 'SPD, Adj for SDE',
                                 'SPD, Adj for SDE & CHR',
                                 'SPD, Adj for SDE, CHR, BMI & SMK'))
  dat
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=Model, y=Est, ymin=LCI, ymax=UCI))+
    geom_pointrange(linetype = 1,size=1.0, colour = "navyblue")+
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept=1), size=1.0, colour="red", lty=2) +
       facet_wrap(~ age, nrow=1)+
    coord_flip()+
    ylim(0,6.0)+
    scale_fill_grey()+ theme_bw()+
    xlab ("  ")+
    ylab("  ")+

theme(text = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),
plot.background = element_rect (),
axis.text.x = element_text(vjust = 1.5, size=18,face="bold"),
axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 1, size=18, face="bold"),
axis.title.y = element_text(hjust=1, size = rel(0.4), face="bold"),
axis.title.x = element_text(vjust=1, size = 20, face = "bold"),
strip.text.x = element_text (size=20, face="bold"),
legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.4), hjust = 0),
legend.position = "none"
)
print(p)
ggsave(file='test_forest_plots_hr.png', width=11, height=7)

messages.subject: Re: Mathematical symbols in legends
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here is a toy example:

DF <- data.frame(age = rpois(40, 55), y = rnorm(40, 10))
DF$Age <- cut(DF$age, c(0, 60, 200), labels = c("< 60", "60+"),
               include.lowest = TRUE)

# Set up legend labels with mathematical symbols
labs <- list(expression(Age < 60), expression(Age >= 60))

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = age, y = y, color = Age)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_color_manual(breaks = levels(DF$Age),
                       values = c("red", "blue"),
                       labels = labs)

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am trying to use the ggplot2 library to create polygon plots with lines overlaid.
I tried two options and have failed at either one to get the complete plots. Could someone please help ?

p = data.frame(x=rep(c(1:3,3:1),4), y=rep(c(4:2,3:5),4), g=rep(c("a","b","c","d"), each=6))
p

n= data.frame(x=c(1,3,1,2,2,3,1,3), y=c(5,2,3,5,4,2,5,2), g=rep(c("a","b","c","d"), each=2))
n

Option one :

pp = ggplot() +
geom_polygon(data=p, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y),
      fill="light blue", alpha = 0.5)+
facet_grid(.~g)
pp

But then how do I add those lines from data=n on these polygon plots ?

Option two :
pp=qplot(data=p,
      x=x,
      y=y,
      geom="polygon",
      facets=~g,  alpha=0.1)+
        geom_polygon(data=p,fill="light blue")
pp
pp+geom_line(data=n, colour="red", size=1, linetype=4)

Here I am unable to get all the panels on the same row (currently it is a 2X2 layout) and the alpha (transparency) option doesn't work properly.

Many Thanks

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I need to get the data from all of the plots I have created. In this case, I have used geom_histogram or geom_boxplot, so I want to know the heights of bars and the box and whisker boundaries. I have seen in posts by others that the function ggplot_build is available to help with this, and does indeed give me the information I need. However, posters have warned using ggplot_build because it was not really intended for this purpose and that it might go away in the future.

So, before I embark on writing code to pull data out using ggplot_build, I am wondering if someone can shed some more light on this concept. Is ggplot_build the best way to do this today? Is there a plan for ggplot_build to go away in the future? Is there a plan to create a different function to provide this data in the future?

Note, I do understand that I could either pre-compute all of the data I have mentioned and plot using that data instead of the raw data or plot the raw data and then post-compute the values I need externally to the plot. However, in both cases that seems to defeat the ease of use of using ggplot to make the plots for you.

Many thanks, and happy new year!
Doug

messages.subject: Re: How do I show striped patterns or any other texture for specific bars when using GGPLOT using example by BRIAN SHINE[Mathematial symbols in legend]
messages.subject_clean: How do I show striped patterns or any other texture for specific bars when using GGPLOT using example by BRIAN SHINE[Mathematial symbols in legend]
messages.body_plain:
Using lines inside of bars or other geoms actually dates back to times before modern screens and printers when the only way to produce a high quality graphic was using a pen plotter.  These were machines that had a robotic arm that picked up a pen and drew the graph on the paper for you.  Because of that there was really only 1 line width available, wider lines were created by drawing the same line multiple times.  In that environment it made sense to not fill an entire rectangle, it was theoretically possible by drawing a bunch of lines really close to each other, but it was really slow (which irritated all the other people waiting to plot something) and often resulted in a hole in the piece of paper rather than something that looked nice.

With modern computers, screens, printers it is much easier to do full color fills so patterns are not really needed unless using a pen plotter.  I have not seen an actual pen plotter in many years, though our family does have a craft machine to cut things from paper/vinyl/etc. which can be converted to a pen plotter (part of me wants to write an R driver to create the old style plots with it, but I would need a lot more spare time and there would be no real benefit).

More recent research (see The Visual Display of Quantitative Information by Tufte, chapter 5) shows that using patterned lines is often more distracting than useful, often producing moire vibration and distorting the relative sizes of bars (poor color choices and other things can also distort relative sizes).  So, it is better not to use lines or hatching in statistical plots (unless your goal is to distort the data and distract the viewer from real information, but if that is the case don't expect us to help).

If color is not available to convey information (and even often when it is) then it may be better to use a different type of plot.  A dotplot may be more useful than a barplot for the example where you can use the point shape to convey information that would require pattern or color in a bar chart.

messages.body_plain:
On 13-01-03 02:02 PM, Greg Snow wrote:
> Using lines inside of bars or other geoms actually dates back to times
> before modern screens and printers when the only way to produce a high
> quality graphic was using a pen plotter.  These were machines that had a
> robotic arm that picked up a pen and drew the graph on the paper for
> you.  Because of that there was really only 1 line width available,
> wider lines were created by drawing the same line multiple times.  In
> that environment it made sense to not fill an entire rectangle, it was
> theoretically possible by drawing a bunch of lines really close to each
> other, but it was really slow (which irritated all the other people
> waiting to plot something) and often resulted in a hole in the piece of
> paper rather than something that looked nice.
>

  On the other hand, I could entertain myself for far too long watching
the plotter do its thing -- put down one color pen, draw a few lines,
pick up another pen ...

> With modern computers, screens, printers it is much easier to do full
> color fills so patterns are not really needed unless using a pen
> plotter.  I have not seen an actual pen plotter in many years, though
> our family does have a craft machine to cut things from paper/vinyl/etc.
> which can be converted to a pen plotter (part of me wants to write an R
> driver to create the old style plots with it, but I would need a lot
> more spare time and there would be no real benefit).
>
> More recent research (see The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
> by Tufte, chapter 5) shows that using patterned lines is often more
> distracting than useful, often producing moire vibration and distorting
> the relative sizes of bars (poor color choices and other things can also
> distort relative sizes).  So, it is better not to use lines or hatching
> in statistical plots (unless your goal is to distort the data and
> distract the viewer from real information, but if that is the case don't
> expect us to help).
>
> If color is not available to convey information (and even often when it
> is) then it may be better to use a different type of plot.  A dotplot
> may be more useful than a barplot for the example where you can use the
> point shape to convey information that would require pattern or color in
> a bar chart.

  There are times when I have wished for pattern fills, for example to
differentiate a couple of different categorical variables (fill color
for one, fill pattern for the other, e.g. species={red,blue},
treatment={open,hashed}.

differences are due to ggplot2 changing. A good way to do this would be
to create a vignette that has all the example code from the book (if
that is even possible given copyright considerations) and then anything
that errors on execution can have its code updated. However, no one has

messages.subject: Re: drawing a multi variable linear line using ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: drawing a multi variable linear line using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

No can do. geom_smooth() only plots 2D lines/curves, not
planes/surfaces in (pseudo-) 3D.  Moreover, the formula has the form y
~ f(x), by which I mean that the formula used must include y as the
response and x as the covariate. One possibility is to try the
scatterplot3d package - its vignette includes an example of how to
plot a plane in a pseudo-3D space.

Dennis

On 1/3/2013 9:29 AM, Ista Zahn wrote:

some hash of the whole legend (or something like that) that was

set when that was a relevant consideration.

messages.body_plain:
Looks like this calls a method from the mgcv library. The formula y~s(x) means to fit a nonparametric smoothing function of x to the data y. The bs="cs" means to use the "cubic spline" basis for the space of functions. Googling "cubic spline" will get you lots of information about the theory.

messages.subject: Re: Group labels ~~a~~ character?
messages.body_plain:
On 1/4/2013 4:06 PM, CShannon wrote:
> This is probably a silly question, but what results in legend labels being
> assigned a coloured dot vs. a coloured ~~a~~ ("a" character, with strike
> through it) symbol in a ggplot2 legend? I assume it's meant to inform on
> the nature of the grouping? Is there anyway to force one or the other?

The elements that appear in the legend (in your example, a colour
legend) correspond to the geoms that use that aesthetic. Different geoms
are represented differently. Consider the following three graphs:

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp, mpg, colour=factor(am)))
p + geom_point()
p + geom_line()
p + geom_text(aes(label=gear))

In all three, there is a colour scale (and legend). The first colors
points and so the legend has a point; the second has colored lines and a
line in the legend; the third has colored text and an "a" in the legend.

Presumably, your graph has both lines and text which is colored so you
get a legend like in this example:

p + geom_line() + geom_text(aes(label=gear))

You can suppress the contribution of a geom to the legend on a per-geom
basis:

p + geom_line() + geom_text(aes(label=gear), show_guide=FALSE)
p + geom_line(show_guide=FALSE) + geom_text(aes(label=gear))
p + geom_line(show_guide=FALSE) + geom_text(aes(label=gear),
show_guide=FALSE)

The last example has no legend because none of the geoms contribute to a
colour legend (though they do use the colour scale).

I don't know a way to add representation to the legend that is not in
the plot (show a point in the legend when there is none in the graph).
You could have a dummy geom_point layer without data and that would work:

p + geom_line(show_guide=FALSE) +
   geom_text(aes(label=gear), show_guide=FALSE) +
   geom_point(data=mtcars[NA_integer_,])

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject_clean: drawing a multi variable linear line using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
I agree you may want to look at alternatives for 3d plotting, but are you perhaps after something as simple as the below.  This is a different interpretation of your question but looking at your code this might be one aspect of what you were heading for.  It doesn't show the model you ask for, but two marginal models instead.  My interpretation is based on the fact that you asked for a "line", and your snippet of code as far as geom_point() is more in tune with what I have below than a three-d picture.

You had a fundamental problem in that you had both of your explanatory variables on the same axis even though they were very different scales, so I have used facets to separate them out.  I have also put them on the horizontal axis which is the usual presentation.  And I have connected together your points (so it becomes a connected scatter plot) to indicate the time series nature of your data

x2.m <- melt(x2, id.vars=c("Date", "Response"))

ggplot(x2.m, aes(x=value, y=Response, color=variable)) +
	geom_point(size=2) +
	geom_line() +
	geom_smooth(method="lm", size=2, lty=2) +
	facet_wrap(~variable, scales="free_x")

PE

Peter Ellis

Hi:

No can do. geom_smooth() only plots 2D lines/curves, not
planes/surfaces in (pseudo-) 3D.  Moreover, the formula has the form y
~ f(x), by which I mean that the formula used must include y as the
response and x as the covariate. One possibility is to try the
scatterplot3d package - its vignette includes an example of how to
plot a plane in a pseudo-3D space.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Data from the created plot - is ggplot_build the best way?
messages.subject_clean: Data from the created plot - is ggplot_build the best way?
messages.body_plain:
> So, before I embark on writing code to pull data out using ggplot_build, I
> am wondering if someone can shed some more light on this concept. Is
> ggplot_build the best way to do this today? Is there a plan for ggplot_build
> to go away in the future? Is there a plan to create a different function to
> provide this data in the future?

It's the best way, if you don't want to precompute the data, but you
need to expect that ggplot_build might change in the future - i.e. it
will be hard to write robust code based on ggplot_build.

> Note, I do understand that I could either pre-compute all of the data I have
> mentioned and plot using that data instead of the raw data or plot the raw
> data and then post-compute the values I need externally to the plot.
> However, in both cases that seems to defeat the ease of use of using ggplot
> to make the plots for you.

If you're going to wrap it in a function, it should be equally easy to
use if you precompute or use ggplot_build, but precomputing will be
much more reliable.  (And the next version of ggplot2 should make it
easier to precompute using the build in statistics)

Hadley

Chief Scientist, RStudio

messages.subject: Custom code: options for left/right/top/bottom axes in ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: Custom code: options for left/right/top/bottom axes in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Dear all (CC Hadley, Winston [at Hadley's suggestion], Jess),

In 2011 I was trying to get ggplot2 to show only left+bottom axes (or other arbitrary combinations of left/right/top/bottom), and came up with this code: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/ggplot2/-ZjRE2OL8lE

The previous code worked with ggplot2 0.8.7, but does not now work with ggplot2 version 0.9.3. The method I was using was to pass a custom object to the "panel.border" option.

In ggplot2 version 0.9.3, to pass something acceptable to theme's "panel.border" option, that something has to be a class inherited from element_rect (checked by validate_element() ) - easy enough. However, if I create an object called MYTHING, then for it to render in ggplot2, I have to have element_grob.MYTHING() be called by ggplot2, and I have failed to achieve this. Specifically, ggplot2's element_render() function calls element_grob(), which uses a UseMethod() call that should call element_grob.SOMETHING(). However, UseMethod() searches within the ggplot2 namespace/environment, so it doesn't find my objects. Moreover, the ggplot2 environment is locked, so I can't add my function to it, and I've found no way round this to allow ggplot2 to find my function in its search/call chain. (Instead, since MYTHING derives from element_rect, then ggplot2's element_grob.element_rect() is called instead.)

On the other hand, I can't find any option to element_rect() to make it draw only some sides of a rectangle -- so I'm stuck.

Have I missed some sensible way to have e.g. only left/bottom sides to panel.border, or to add things to ggplot2's call chain?

Many thanks!

All the best,
Rudolf.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Baptiste,

Thank you! That worked a treat; hardly ugly.
The revised code is at http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes_2013_01.r and pasted below.

All the best,
Rudolf.

# Rudolf Cardinal, March 2011
# Simple extensions to ggplot2 (v0.8.7); see http://pobox.com/~rudolf/statistics/R
# Modified 5 Jan 2013 for ggplot2 0.9.3 (NB: use sessionInfo() to find current package versions)
# - fetch ggplot2 source with: git clone https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2.git
# Changes, because ggplot2 has changed its internal calling mechanisms:
# - opts() deprecated in favour of theme()
# - "Element panel.border must be an element_rect object" (error from validate_element() in theme-elements.r)
#   ... so change all class = "theme" to class = c("element_rect", "element")
# - "cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'list'"
#   ... a closure is a function (see ?typeof)
#   ... change class to be of class c("MYCLASS", "element_rect", "element")
# - then element_grob.MYCLASS not called by element_render()/element_grob()/UseMethod()... environment/namespace problem
#   tried setMethod("element_grob", "theme_border", function(STUFF) { STUFF} , where = as.environment("package:ggplot2")
#   but the environment is locked
#   ggplot2's theme-elements.r defines e.g. element_rect (exported) and element_grob.element_rect (not exported, does the work)
#   However, we can't override an internal function:
#       ... e.g. rewrite "validate_element" to crash
#           set environment(validate_element) <- as.environment("package:ggplot2") -- doesn't break the plotting.
# - Upshot: now impossible to hack through this way (locked environment).
# - http://obeautifulcode.com/R/How-R-Searches-And-Finds-Stuff/
# - http://stackoverflow.com/questions/8204008/redirect-intercept-function-calls-within-a-package-function
# - These don't fix it:
#   library(proto)
#   theme <- with(proto(environment(ggplot2::theme), theme = ggplot2::theme, element_grob.theme_border = my.element_grob.theme_border), theme) --- doesn't work
#   ggplot <- with(proto(environment(ggplot2::ggplot), ggplot = ggplot2::ggplot, element_grob.theme_border = my.element_grob.theme_border), ggplot) --- breaks!
# - Fix by Baptiste Auguie 8/1/2013: inherit from element_blank instead; then it works fine.

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Requirements
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(grid) # for gpar

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Code duplicated from ggplot2 source (not exposed to wider namespace) for convenience
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

.pt <- 1 / 0.352777778
len0_null <- function(x) {
    if (length(x) == 0)  NULL
    else                 x
}

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Generic panel border (can set any combination of left/right/top/bottom)
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

theme_border <- function(
        type = c("left", "right", "bottom", "top", "none"),
        colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
    # use with e.g.: ggplot(...) + opts( panel.border=theme_border(type=c("bottom","left")) ) + ...
    type <- match.arg(type, several.ok=TRUE)
    structure(
        list(type = type, colour = colour, size = size, linetype = linetype),
        class = c("theme_border", "element_blank", "element")
    )
}
element_grob.theme_border <- function(
        element, x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1,
        type = NULL,
        colour = NULL, size = NULL, linetype = NULL,
        ...) {
    if (is.null(type)) type = element$type
    xlist <- c()
    ylist <- c()
    idlist <- c()
    if ("bottom" %in% type) { # bottom
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x, x+width))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y, y))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(1,1))
    }
    if ("top" %in% type) { # top
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x, x+width))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y+height, y+height))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(2,2))
    }
    if ("left" %in% type) { # left
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x, x))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y, y+height))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(3,3))
    }
    if ("right" %in% type) { # right
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x+width, x+width))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y, y+height))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(4,4))
    }
    if (length(type)==0 || "none" %in% type) { # blank; cannot pass absence of coordinates, so pass a single point and use an invisible line
        xlist <- c(x,x)
        ylist <- c(y,y)
        idlist <- c(5,5)
        linetype <- "blank"
    }
    gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(size * .pt), col = colour, lty = linetype)
    element_gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(element$size * .pt), col = element$colour, lty = element$linetype)
    polylineGrob(
        x = xlist, y = ylist, id = idlist, ..., default.units = "npc",
        gp = modifyList(element_gp, gp),
    )
}

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For convenience: "L" (left + bottom) border
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

theme_L_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
    # use with e.g.: ggplot(...) + theme( panel.border=theme_L_border() ) + ...
    structure(
        list(colour = colour, size = size, linetype = linetype),
        class = c("theme_L_border", "element_blank", "element")
    )
}
element_grob.theme_L_border <- function(
        element, x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1,
        colour = NULL, size = NULL, linetype = NULL,
        ...) {
    gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(size * .pt), col = colour, lty = linetype)
    element_gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(element$size * .pt), col = element$colour, lty = element$linetype)
    polylineGrob(
        x = c(x+width, x, x), y = c(y,y,y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
        gp = modifyList(element_gp, gp),
    )
}

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For convenience: bottom border only
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

theme_bottom_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
    # use with e.g.: ggplot(...) + theme( panel.border=theme_bottom_border() ) + ...
    structure(
        list(colour = colour, size = size, linetype = linetype),
        class = c("theme_bottom_border", "element_blank", "element")
    )
}
element_grob.theme_bottom_border <- function(
        element, x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1,
        colour = NULL, size = NULL, linetype = NULL,
        ...) {
    gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(size * .pt), col = colour, lty = linetype)
    element_gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(element$size * .pt), col = element$colour, lty = element$linetype)
    polylineGrob(
        x = c(x, x+width), y = c(y,y), ..., default.units = "npc",
        gp = modifyList(element_gp, gp),
    )
}

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For convenience: left border only
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

theme_left_border <- function(colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
    # use with e.g.: ggplot(...) + theme( panel.border=theme_left_border() ) + ...
    structure(
        list(colour = colour, size = size, linetype = linetype),
        class = c("theme_left_border", "element_blank", "element")
    )
}
element_grob.theme_left_border <- function(
        element, x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1,
        colour = NULL, size = NULL, linetype = NULL,
        ...) {
    gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(size * .pt), col = colour, lty = linetype)
    element_gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(element$size * .pt), col = element$colour, lty = element$linetype)
    polylineGrob(
        x = c(x, x), y = c(y, y+height), ..., default.units = "npc",
        gp = modifyList(element_gp, gp),
    )
}

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Border selection by number
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

theme_border_numerictype <- function(type, colour = "black", size = 1, linetype = 1) {
    # use with e.g.: ggplot(...) + theme( panel.border=theme_border(type=9) ) + ...
    structure(
        list(type = type, colour = colour, size = size, linetype = linetype),
        class = c("theme_border_numerictype", "element_blank", "element")
    )
}
element_grob.theme_border_numerictype <- function(
        element, x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1,
        type = NULL,
        colour = NULL, size = NULL, linetype = NULL,
        ...) {
    if (is.null(type)) type = element$type
    # numerical types from: library(gridExtra); example(borderGrob)
    # 1=none, 2=bottom, 3=right, 4=top, 5=left, 6=B+R, 7=T+R, 8=T+L, 9=B+L, 10=T+B, 11=L+R, 12=T+B+R, 13=T+L+R, 14=T+B+L, 15=B+L+R, 16=T+B+L+R
    xlist <- c()
    ylist <- c()
    idlist <- c()
    if (type==2 || type==6 || type==9 || type==10 || type==12 || type==14 || type==15 || type==16) { # bottom
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x, x+width))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y, y))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(1,1))
    }
    if (type==4 || type==7 || type==8 || type==10 || type==12 || type==13 || type==14 || type==16) { # top
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x, x+width))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y+height, y+height))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(2,2))
    }
    if (type==5 || type==8 || type==9 || type==11 || type==13 || type==14 || type==15 || type==16) { # left
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x, x))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y, y+height))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(3,3))
    }
    if (type==3 || type==6 || type==7 || type==11 || type==12 || type==13 || type==15 || type==16) { # right
        xlist <- append(xlist, c(x+width, x+width))
        ylist <- append(ylist, c(y, y+height))
        idlist <- append(idlist, c(4,4))
    }
    if (type==1) { # blank; can't pass absence of coordinates, so pass a single point and use an invisible line
        xlist <- c(x,x)
        ylist <- c(y,y)
        idlist <- c(5,5)
        linetype <- "blank"
    }
    gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(size * .pt), col = colour, lty = linetype)
    element_gp <- gpar(lwd = len0_null(element$size * .pt), col = element$colour, lty = element$linetype)
    polylineGrob(
        x = xlist, y = ylist, id = idlist, ..., default.units = "npc",
        gp = modifyList(element_gp, gp),
    )
}

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Examples
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

rnc_ggplot2_border_themes_example_script = '
    library(ggplot2)
    df = data.frame( x=c(1,2,3), y=c(4,5,6) )
    source("http://egret.psychol.cam.ac.uk/statistics/R/extensions/rnc_ggplot2_border_themes_2013_01.r")
    ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + theme( panel.border = theme_border( c("bottom","left") ) )
    ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + theme( panel.border = theme_left_border() )
    ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + theme( panel.border = theme_bottom_border() )
    ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + theme( panel.border = theme_L_border() )
    ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + theme( panel.border = theme_border_numerictype(12) ) # use 1:16 as possible values
'

messages.subject: Re: Control jitter for overlaying plots
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Winston.  I was able to something working with discrete data.  Here is some code that provides an example of a plot.  There may be a more elegant way to do this, but it this works:

x=rbinom(100,1,.5)
y=rnorm(100,50,5)
z=rbinom(100,1,.2)

j.x = jitter(x,factor=.2) + 1
j.xz = ifelse(z,j.x,NA)

testdat = data.frame(x,y,j.x,j.xz)
dummy = data.frame(x=c(0,1),y=c(50,60),grp=c(1,1))

ggplot(data=testdat) +
  geom_point(aes(x=j.x,y=y),colour="blue",size=2,shape=19) + # Plot all x's (jittered)
  geom_point(aes(x=j.xz,y=y),colour="red",size=4,shape=1) +  # Circle x's with z=1 (same jitter)
  geom_path(data=dummy,aes(x=factor(x),y=y,group=grp),linetype=0) + # Forces the x-axis to only 2 factors
  scale_y_continuous() +
  scale_x_discrete()

messages.subject: Histogram binwidth by facet?
messages.body_plain:
Hey there!

I'm trying to produce a plot showing the effect of a tranformation of my response variable. I do this by plotting histograms of the raw and transformed data. The default, range/30 gives too many bins. But setting the binwidth in the geom_histogram call sets a universal binwidth across both facets, which is not the result I want.

How do I set binwidth according to a factor? (In this case, the same factor that I am facetting by.)

Minimal working example, with some silly data:

##
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape)
data <- seq(from=0,to=0.2,length=100) #raw response
trans <- log(data/(1-data)) #logit transformed response
frame <- melt(data.frame(data,trans)) #collect
ggplot(data = frame, aes(x=value)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") #default - too many bins, but they are nicel adjusted for each facet.
ggplot(data = frame, aes(x=value)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = diff(range(dat$value))/5) + facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") #what I want - but I want the binwidth to be 1/5 of the range *within each facet*
##

Thanks in advance!
Benjamin

messages.subject: Re: graphing time data on x and y axis?
messages.subject_clean: graphing time data on x and y axis?
messages.body_plain:
I think part of the problem is that you don't have you date's properly formated. See this blog post for some help. Once you get your dates in the right format, you're going to have to use the new scales package to get the format and breaks that you're after. Sadly, it's not something I do a lot so we'll need more help.

Something like:

yy$Date<-as.POSIXct(yy$Date, format="%Y-%m-%d")

yy$STime<-as.POSIXct(yy$STime, format="%H:%M")
yy$ETime<-as.POSIXct(yy$ETime, format="%H:%M")

ggplot(yy, aes(Date, ETime, group="Team")) +
geom_jitter() +
facet_wrap( ~ Team) +
geom_hline(yintercept=yy$Stime, colour="red", size=2)

#Except it errors out because your data is all the same
#Error in prettyDate(x = x, n = n, min.n = min.n, sep = sep, ...) :
# range too small for min.n

messages.subject: Re: step function with confidence interval shaded
messages.subject_clean: step function with confidence interval shaded
messages.body_plain:
Sorry to revive a dead thread, but it comes up high when searching for step ribbons. I constructed a stat_stepribbon function that seems to be working well for me that answers your desire for a "stat_step" for ribbons. ("stat_step" would seem to be logical for lines, but there is already a perfectly functional geom_step that works fine for that purpose.)

See this thread: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/ggplot2/9cFWHaH1CPs

On Wednesday, March 17, 2010 3:40:25 PM UTC-7, Brian Diggs wrote:
>
> On Mar 17, 11:43 am, wcyee <wcy...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi - What is a good way of plotting a step function with upper/lower
> > bounds shaded (as in geom_smooth, for example)?
> >
> > For example, I can plot:
> >
> > x <- 1:10
> > df <- data.frame(x=x, y=x+10, ymin=x+7, ymax=x+12)
> > p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_step()
> > p + geom_step(aes(x, ymin, linetype=2), data=df) + geom_step(aes(x,
> > ymax, linetype=2), data=df)
> > print(p)
> >
> > How would I shade the area between ymin and ymax?
> >
> > At first I thought I would experiment with geom_ribbon or geom_smooth
> > in conjunction with stat_step.  But it seems there's no such object
> > "stat_step" even though google turns up some references in a
> > "changelog".  (I'm using ggplot2 0.8.5)
> >
> > Aside, I only started learning ggplot2 recently and everything they
> > say is really true: it's very cool!
> >
> > Thanks much for any help!
>
> Despite the changelog entry, there doesn't seem to be a stat_step.
> There is a stairstep function, but it makes a lot of assumptions.
> This is a cobbled together approach; it transforms the data.frame
> using a variant of the stairstep function, and then plots using that
> transformed data.frame.  "Ugly hack" might be a generous description.
> Better, more elegant solutions welcome; a real stat_step very welcome.
>
> stairstep.name <http://stairstep.name> <- function(df, direction, x.name <http://x.name>, y.name <http://y.name>) {
>         df[["x"]] <- df[[x.name <http://x.name>]]
>         df[["y"]] <- df[[y.name <http://y.name>]]
>         ss <- stairstep(df, direction=direction)
>         ret.df <- data.frame(ss[["x"]],ss[["y"]])
>         names(ret.df) <- c(x.name <http://x.name>, y.name <http://y.name>)
>         rownames(ret.df) <- rownames(ss)
>         ret.df
> }
>
> step.df <- Reduce(merge,alply(setdiff(names(df),"x"), 1, function(y)
> {stairstep.name <http://stairstep.name>(df, "hv", "x", y)}))
>
> ggplot(step.df, aes(x,y)) + geom_smooth(aes(ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax),
> stat="identity")
>
> --Brian Diggs
>

messages.subject: Re: With stat="summary", fun.y="mean" get "Each group consist of only one observation"
messages.subject_clean: With stat="summary", fun.y="mean" get "Each group consist of only one observation"
messages.body_plain:
Since the stat_summary() examples in the current documentation
indicate the same error message, the safe thing to do in the interim
is probably to do the summarization outside of ggplot2 in a separate
data frame and then use it in the layers where you need it.

Here is an example for a simple interaction plot:

library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)

# Produce a data frame of mean(mpg) for vs/am combinations
mtm <- ddply(mtcars, .(vs, am), summarise, mn = mean(mpg))

# interaction plot
ggplot(mtm, aes(x = factor(vs), y = mn, group = factor(am))) +
     geom_point(size = 3) + geom_line()

# The error message appears if I try something like this in 0.9.3:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(vs), y = mpg) +
    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, aes(group = factor(am)),
                          geom = "point", size = 3) +
    stat_summary(fun.y = mean, aes(group = factor(am)),
                          geom = "line", size = 1)

The first stat_summary() call works, but not the second.

I looked around yesterday for open or closed issues on GitHub
regarding this topic, but didn't find one, so I don't know offhand if
this has been fixed in the development version or not.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Histogram binwidth by facet?
messages.body_plain:
Le mercredi 9 janvier 2013 11:34:11 UTC+1, skipperhoyer a écrit :
> Hey there!
>
> I'm trying to produce a plot showing the effect of a tranformation of my response variable. I do this by plotting histograms of the raw and transformed data. The default, range/30 gives too many bins. But setting the binwidth in the geom_histogram call sets a universal binwidth across both facets, which is not the result I want.
>
> How do I set binwidth according to a factor? (In this case, the same factor that I am facetting by.)
>
> Minimal working example, with some silly data:
>
> ##
> library(ggplot2)
> library(reshape)
> data <- seq(from=0,to=0.2,length=100) #raw response
> trans <- log(data/(1-data)) #logit transformed response
> frame <- melt(data.frame(data,trans)) #collect
> ggplot(data = frame, aes(x=value)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") #default - too many bins, but they are nicel adjusted for each facet.
> ggplot(data = frame, aes(x=value)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = diff(range(dat$value))/5) + facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") #what I want - but I want the binwidth to be 1/5 of the range *within each facet*
> ##
>

Hi Benjamin,

You could find another solution in this <https://groups.google.com/d/topic/ggplot2/aQQ2hTYRQF8/discussion> subject : multiple calls to the same geom allow the use of different bins.

Pierre

> have shape=16 and size=2.

> update_geom_defaults("boxplot",
>                       list(colour='blue', outlier.shape=1, outlier.size=5))
>
> ggplot(diamonds, aes(depth, carat)) + geom_boxplot()
>
> So, it seems that the default values of outlier parameters are not updated
> by update_geom_defaults. I would consider this a bug.

It is not really a bug, but it does look like one (and maybe things
should be changed so that it does work this way).  update_geom_defaults
updates the default values that an aesthetic will take when it is not
mapped to a variable. In geom_boxplot, the aesthetics are listed as:
lower, middle, upper, x, ymax, ymin, alpha, colour, fill, linetype,
shape, size, and weight. outlier.colour, outlier.shape, and outlier.size
are not aesthetics but rather arguments to geom_boxplot. That means that
they can not be mapped to a variable, but it also means that their
default values can not be changed by update_geom_defaults. It also means
that the value of those must be the same for an entire layer.

> Sorry if this isn't the right place to report bugs.

The bug reporting system is at https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues

However, it is fine to inquire here on the mailing list if you are not
sure if something is a bug or if something does not behave as you
expect. If it is a bug, then you may be asked to file a formal bug
report, but if it is not then it does not clutter the bug database.

messages.subject: Re: image type
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

When using a bitmap format like png, the most important thing is the
resolution. The tradeoff is that the better the resolution the bigger
the file. Here are some examples:

library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars,
            aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) +
  geom_point()

png("pngDefault.png")
p
dev.off()

png("png_6X6_res_300.png", width = 6, height = 6, res=300, units="in")
p
dev.off()

png("png_6X6_res_600.png", width = 6, height = 6, res=600, units="in")
p
dev.off()

ggsave("ggsaveDefault.png", plot=p)

ggsave("ggsave_6X6.png", width = 6, height = 6, plot=p)

ggsave("ggsave_6X6_dpi_600.png", width = 6, height = 6, dpi=600, plot=p)

grep("png", system("ls -l", intern=TRUE), value=TRUE)
## [1] "-rw-r--r-- 1 izahn users    98653 Jan 12 12:36 ggsave_6X6_dpi_600.png"
## [2] "-rw-r--r-- 1 izahn users    34392 Jan 12 12:36 ggsave_6X6.png"
## [3] "-rw-r--r-- 1 izahn users    44820 Jan 12 12:36 ggsaveDefault.png"
## [4] "-rw-r--r-- 1 izahn users    34392 Jan 12 12:35 png_6X6_res_300.png"
## [5] "-rw-r--r-- 1 izahn users    98653 Jan 12 12:35 png_6X6_res_600.png"
## [6] "-rw-r--r-- 1 izahn users     4390 Jan 12 12:35 pngDefault.png"

Viewing thes images in Firefox I find that all but pngDefault look
reasonably sharp. The fonts look somewhat better on the ggsave
versions, but that could be my eyes playing tricks on me. When viewing
in Firefox the 600 dpi images look great at full size, but no so good
when scaled down, so you might try saving to a smaller size (but
keeping high resolution). In terms of size even largest on is only 96
KiB, which is not really that big for modern browsers/networks. Of
course if you have 50 of these on a page that will add up quick...

Hope this helps!
Ista

I have also had some good luck with SVG for online graphics.  They
work pretty well in recent browser versions of at least Firefox,
Chrome, IE (9 & 10), and Safari.

Of course you can also up the resolution as Ista showed you.  I will
point out that depending on the elements of the image, vector graphics
can be huge or small.  For example a barplot with three bars may be
quite small in vector graphics.  A scatter plot with 15 million points
will be a nightmare and you would almost certainly want to
pre-rasterize that (not serve the data and force poor users' browsers
to do that).

This strays from ggplot2, but if you have many of these on a single
webpage and typical users are only interested in a handful, you might
serving thumbnails on the initial page that when clicked take you to
the full image.  This can speed things up for your users and decrease
the bandwidth you are using.  Just as a quick example of how easy
these are to automatically make, I have three test images from R in
various resolutions and dimensions, which I want to scale all to have
about a total of 10000 pixels

if I focus on a defined interval to plot my data (e.g. scale_x_continuous or xlim) I still have a y-axis that comprises the range of the complete dataset. I would like the y-axis to be restricted in respect to my choice of xlim or scale_x_continuous).

scale_*_continuous() and xlim()/ylim() only restrict axes in one
dimension. If you subset your data, you get exactly what you want:

ggplot(subset(dft, n <= 4)) + geom_point(aes(x = n, y = m))

messages.subject: Re: y-axis too big after xlim
messages.body_plain:
Here's one solution to your problem, Hermann.

Use of coord_cartesian() for zooming:
http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3/coord_cartesian.html

########################
####   Your examples   ####
########################
#  Remove all objects from workspace
rm(list = ls())

#  Load ggplot2 library
library(ggplot2)

#  Prepare data.frame
dft <- structure(list(n = 1:10,

                      m = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 100, 20, 18, 16)),
                      .Names = c("n", "m"),
                      row.names = c(NA, -10L),
                      class = "data.frame")

#  Confirm data.frame structure
str(dft)

#  First plot example with xlim()
ggplot (dft) +
  geom_point (aes (x=n, y=m)) +
  xlim (c (1,5))

#  Second plot example with scale_x_continuous()
ggplot (dft) +
  geom_point (aes (x=n, y=m)) +
  scale_x_continuous (limits = c(1,4))

##########################
######  end examples  ######
##########################

##########################
####  Possible solutions  ####
##########################
#  Using coord_cartesian() for zooming
#  x-axis restricted to 0 and 5 (xlim)
#  y-axis restricted to 0 and 10 (ylim)
ggplot (dft) +
  geom_point (aes (x=n, y=m)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5), ylim = c(0,10)) +
  ggtitle("Using coord_cartesian as a zooming function\nExample 1")

#  Using coord_cartesian() for zooming
#  x-axis restricted to 0 and 4 (xlim)
#  y-axis restricted to 0 and 8 (ylim)
ggplot (dft) +
  geom_point(aes (x = n, y = m)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 4), ylim = c(0, 8)) +
  ggtitle('Using coord_cartesian as a zooming function\nExample 2')

#  Alternatively, you could also place the data object and primary aesthetics inside of ggplot() and
#  fine tune your plot with breaks, labels and a title like so...
ggplot (dft, aes(n, m)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_point() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5.25), ylim = c(0, 10.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,12, by = 1.0)) +
  labs(x = 'n', y = 'm') +
  ggtitle('Using coord_cartesian as a zooming function\nExample 3')

##########################
##### end pos_solutions  ####
##########################

Hope this helps.

Derek

messages.subject: Re: biexponential scale
messages.body_plain:
Anja,

I think the point of the new scales package is that you can define the scales in any way you want. How exactly you go about doing that is a question I'm not skilled enough to answer. I would suggest digesting the scales package documentation a bit, and/or hope that someone with the skills can chime in and help.

require(scales)
?scales
?trans_new

log_trans
#so you can see the guts of a trans

function (base = exp(1))
{
    trans <- function(x) log(x, base)
    inv <- function(x) base^x
    trans_new(str_c("log-", format(base)), trans, inv, log_breaks(base = base),
        domain = c(1e-100, Inf))
}
<environment: namespace:scales>

Brandon

messages.subject: why theme_bw changes font size?
messages.body_plain:
I just noticed that theme_bw() changes font size to `rel(0.8)` (see source). What's the reasoning behind a (non specialized) theme changing font size? For example, I would understand if a theme were to emulate a specific graphic from a journal that demands a certain font type, but I would not expect a black & white theme to touch the font size.

This is somewhat frustrating when one doesn't realize that the order of calling functions matters. For example, calling `theme(text = element_text(size = 15))` before theme_bw() has no effect, hot blood is spilled and I get flak for how R can't handle basic graphs. :)

Cheers,
Roman

Are you referring to

function (base_size = 12, base_family = "")
{
<snip>
        theme(axis.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8)), axis.ticks =
element_line(colour = "black"),
<snip>
}

? If so, the default theme_gray does this as well, so it's not really
changing the default, but maintaining it.

> What's the reasoning behind a (non specialized) theme changing font size?
> For example, I would understand if a theme were to emulate a specific
> graphic from a journal that demands a certain font type, but I would not
> expect a black & white theme to touch the font size.

Well, it has to have a value. And it is set the the same value as in
the default theme.

>
> This is somewhat frustrating when one doesn't realize that the order of
> calling functions matters. For example, calling `theme(text =
> element_text(size = 15))` before theme_bw() has no effect, hot blood is
> spilled and I get flak for how R can't handle basic graphs. :)

Well, now you know. Since themes can set all kinds of things, you
should always put things intended to override theme settings after
calling the theme.

Hi Brandon
Thanks for your reply.
I have had a further play with the code and found that when I comment out vertical bars (indicating 2 time points when Christchurch was hit by major earthquakes) the code now runs.  So at the risk of getting this completely wrong (and ignoring your request above- sorry Brandon), I am posting the code that is used to make the vertical lines below.  If this is commented out, the graph runs fine.

this is the code to load the EQ data:

# Load EQ and colours
load("colourEQ.RData", .GlobalEnv)
#this is code in the ggplot statement
geom_vline(data = EQ, colour = colourEQ, linetype = "dashed", aes(xintercept = start )) +

plot1 <- ggplot()+
  theme_bw() +
  #geom_rect(data = EQmonth3roll, fill = colourEQ , aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf)) +
  geom_vline(data = EQ, colour = colourEQ, linetype = "dashed", aes(xintercept = start )) +
  geom_line(data = data1, colour=coloursingle , size=1, aes(x = datemonth, y = count) ) +
  ylabel1 +
  yfont +
  xlabel +
  title1 +
  legend +
  facet_grid(area ~., scale="free_y")
plot1

It is stored in a common file that is loaded by:
# Load EQ and colours
load("colourEQ.RData", .GlobalEnv)

#code from common file#
#
# Set up earthquake data
#
#
##### SET UP #####
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
# load the necessary libraries
library(lubridate)
# Set paths and macros
kBaseDir   <- file.path("//corp.ssi.govt.nz/shared/CERA/Community <http://corp.ssi.govt.nz/shared/CERA/Community> Wellbeing/Social Outcomes Framework/Indicators/Common")
#Change to the new directory
setwd(kBaseDir)

##### BUILD EARTHQUAKE DATASETS #####
# Dates (one day)
EQ <- read.csv("EQ_dates.csv")
EQ$start <- dmy(EQ$start)
EQ
# Monthly
EQmonth <- read.csv("EQ_dates_monthly.csv")
EQmonth$start <- dmy(EQmonth$start)
EQmonth$end <- dmy(EQmonth$end)
EQmonth
# Monthly, 3 month rolling (ie quarter ending month)
EQmonth3roll <- read.csv("EQ_dates_monthly3roll.csv")
EQmonth3roll$start <- dmy(EQmonth3roll$start)
EQmonth3roll$end <- dmy(EQmonth3roll$end)
EQmonth3roll

# Quarterly
EQquarter <- read.csv("EQ_dates_quarterly.csv")
EQquarter$start <- dmy(EQquarter$start)
EQquarter$end <- dmy(EQquarter$end)
EQquarter
# Monthly - for bar charts
EQmonth_bar <- read.csv("EQ_dates_monthly_bar.csv")
EQmonth_bar
# Yearly
EQyear <- read.csv("EQ_dates_yearly.csv")
EQyear$start <- dmy(EQyear$start)
EQyear$end <- dmy(EQyear$end)
EQyear
# Yearly, year ending June
EQyearendjune <- read.csv("EQ_dates_year_end_june.csv")
EQyearendjune$start <- dmy(EQyearendjune$start)
EQyearendjune$end <- dmy(EQyearendjune$end)
EQyearendjune

# Yearly, year ending each quarter
EQyearendquarter <- read.csv("EQ_dates_year_end_quarter.csv")
EQyearendquarter$start <- dmy(EQyearendquarter$start)
EQyearendquarter$end <- dmy(EQyearendquarter$end)
EQyearendquarter

##### SAVE DATA WITH EARTHQUAKE INFO#####
save(colourEQ,coloursingle,colours,EQ, EQmonth,EQquarter,EQmonth_bar, EQyear,EQyearendjune,EQyearendquarter,EQmonth3roll,  file= "colourEQ.RData")
# To load that set of saved data
# rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
# load("colourEQ.RData", .GlobalEnv)

# END OF FILE

As I said, this is the code in the plot code:

# Load EQ and colours
load("colourEQ.RData", .GlobalEnv)
geom_vline(data = EQ, colour = colourEQ, linetype = "dashed", aes(xintercept = start )) +
this code in the plot calls up vertical lines indicating dates of quakes so viewers can gauge activity before and after the 2 main quakes. I left this code out of the original post to avoid complicating an already complicated question, but now it seems to be the issue.
the data 'EQ' is a csv file that contains the following:'
startevent
4/09/20101
22/02/20112
----

geom_vline(data = EQ, colour = colourEQ, linetype = "dashed", aes(xintercept = start )) +
if the above code is commented out, the graph is fine (minus the vertical 'EQ' lines of course)  but if included, the following error message is displayed:

Error: Discrete value supplied to continuous scale

hope this makes some kind of sense?

regards,
Mark

messages.subject: Problem with scales in facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to plot relationships between observed and expected values
for a number of metrics at different subsets of sites.
These metrics have different scales (some unbound, others from zero to
one), so having free scales is essential.

If I use facet_grid(Metric~SiteSet, scales="free"), only one axis will
have free scales. Specifically, the y-axis. If I flip it around and use
facet_grid(SiteSet~Metric, scales="free"), only the x-axis will be free.

If I use facet_wrap, both scales are truly free, but I lose the
structure I wanted.

I suppose I could use facet wrap and force the panel ordering using
factor(), but does anyone know if this is a bug in facet_grid, or am I
doing something wrong?

--
Raphael Mazor

Mark,

I would say that it's the format of your date column in the EQ dataframe. If it is being stored as a character (or in this case a factor) and you are trying to align that to other data which is stored as.Date() then it will not know what to do. Make sure the format between EQ and your other datasets are the same.

Brandon

messages.body_plain:
Sorry. Here's a reproducible example:

mydata<-data.frame(SiteSet=rep(c("SetA","SetB","SetC"), each = 200),
                   Metric=rep(c("Metric1","Metric2"), each=100))
mydata$Observed<-ifelse(mydata$Metric=="Metric1", runif(100,min=0,max=1), runif(100,min=0,max=100))
mydata$Expected<-ifelse(mydata$Metric=="Metric1", runif(100,min=0,max=1), runif(100,min=0,max=100))

ggplot(data=mydata, aes(x=Expected,y=Observed))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_grid(Metric~SiteSet, scales="free")

I get the following graph:

If i flip facet grid as follows, I get a different, but also wrong result:
ggplot(data=mydata, aes(x=Expected,y=Observed))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_grid(SiteSet~Metric, scales="free")

If I use facet_wrap, the scales are correct, but I lose the gridded structure. For this example, it's not a problem, but my real data is a bit more complex:

mydata$MetricSiteSet<-paste(mydata$Metric,mydata$SiteSet, sep=".")
ggplot(data=mydata, aes(x=Expected,y=Observed))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~MetricSiteSet, scales="free")

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Thanks for the example. It makes the problem much clearer to see.

The problem is that faceted 2D plots by facet_grid() cannot have separate, "free" x and y axis pairs in each panel, as you discovered - the y-axis in each row needs to be consistent and the x-axis in each column needs to be the same. You have such a structure marginally - i.e., you have consistent x/y axes for Metric1 and the same for Metric2 - but the x/y-axes differ for Metric1 and Metric2.

I think there is a compromise solution that is fairly easy to produce using the gridExtra package - I don't know whether or not you'll find it satisfactory for your 'real' problem, though.

library(ggplot2)

mydata<-data.frame(SiteSet=rep(c("SetA","SetB","SetC"), each = 200),
                   Metric=rep(c("Metric1","Metric2"), each=100))
mydata$Observed<-ifelse(mydata$Metric=="Metric1", runif(100,min=0,max=1), runif(100,min=0,max=100))
mydata$Expected<-ifelse(mydata$Metric=="Metric1", runif(100,min=0,max=1), runif(100,min=0,max=100))

# Split into two data frames, one for Metric1 data and another for Metric2.
# Redefine the factors so that the resulting Metric factor has one level.
metric1 <- subset(mydata, Metric == "Metric1")
metric1$Metric <- factor(metric1$Metric)
metric2 <- subset(mydata, Metric == "Metric2")
metric2$Metric <- factor(metric2$Metric)

Each of these produces a three row, one column grid of plots:

p1 <- ggplot(metric1, aes(x = Expected, y = Observed)) +
         geom_point() +
         facet_grid(SiteSet ~ Metric)

# same plot code as p1, just substituting the input data frame
p2 <- p1 %+% metric2

# Put the two graphs side-by-side:
library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)

The result is two grids instead of one, but the scales are self-consistent within graph.

If you want to get rid of the y-axis label in p2, use

p2 <- p1 %+% metric2 + ylab(NULL)

HTH,
Dennis

Hi,

On 1 January 2013 13:15, baptiste auguie <baptist...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I'm compiling examples for a talk on producing scientific graphs in physics and chemistry. I will present 'the good, the bad, and the ugly' as a means of introduction to best practices and mistakes to avoid when making a plot, regardless of the tool being used. Maybe I'll have a few slides with the original bad graph, and a proposed improvement next to it. Of course being a ggplot2 user, I only have vague memories of truly bad and ugly graphics. Would you have a link to share presenting such examples, along the lines of Tufte's books but online?
>
> Things that come to mind in no particular order,
>
> - 3D pie chart
> - some 2D pie charts
> - 3D barplots
> - double-axis
> - misleading axes, and scales
> - inappropriate colours
> - ugly fonts
> - useless "decorations" such as shadows, background image, etc.
> - uninformative legend
> - plot with too much information (wrong type of plot)
> - export in lossy jpeg format
> - manual tweaking of data points / scales
>
>
> Cheers, and a Happy New Year!
>
> baptiste
>
>

These are messages informing you that ggplot2 is using gam() to create
the smoothing rather than loess.

> geom_smooth: method="auto" and size of largest group is >=1000, so using gam
> with formula: y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"). Use 'method = x' to change the smoothing
> method.
> geom_smooth: method="auto" and size of largest group is <1000, so using
> loess. Use 'method = x' to change the smoothing method.

This is definitely an error, but it's informative:

> Error in predLoess(object$y, object$x, newx, object$s, object$weights,  :
>   NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 5)

arg 5 is weights, and it's telling you that at least one of the
weights either blew up (Inf), generated an NaN or a missing value (not
uncommon along the extremes if the data in those regions is too
sparse).

> In addition: There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first
> 50)
> Error in if (nrow(layer_data) == 0) return() : argument is of length zero

This warning appears to be indicating that at least one of your groups
has no data, but a traceback of the call may be more informative.

>
> I tried uninstalling and reinstalling ggplot2
>
> Code:
> bpssc <- read.csv ("bp-join.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",", quote="\"",
> dec=".",fill = FALSE,colClasses=c("Date"="Date"))

> ggplot<- ggplot(data=bpssc, aes(x=Date,y=BR.Score, group = Unit))

> scale_colour_brewer(type="qual", palette="Dark2")

> last_plot() + stat_smooth(aes(group = 1),fill = "darkgray",
> se=TRUE,col="black", size = .9, level =.95,fullrange = FALSE,lty=2) #group 1

>
> last_plot() + stat_smooth(aes(color = BR.Region),fill = "darkgray", se=F,
> size = 1.9, level =.95,fullrange = TRUE)#trends of individual regions

One guess is that because of the fullrange argument, at least one of
your groups had little or no data in the extremes of the x-range,
which causes the loess/gam algorithm to become sufficiently unstable
to generate NA/NaN/Inf weights. Remember that warning in intro stats
about extrapolating beyond the range of your data? When dealing with
adaptive estimation algorithms, this warning is especially true.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

Thanks, the first blog post is very clear and helpful! I've tried to create a biexponential transformation building upon your example. A conditional transformation of the values did work, but the scale itself remained the same, so that e.g. 1000 became 3 (log-transformed) and was plotted at the break "3". The problem is that I want the original data values to remain the same (so 1000 should still be 1000 rather than 3) while the scale format should change from linear to logarithmic halfway through. So I guess it's more a matter of the breaks and format functions rather than transformation, right? However, I still don't have a clue how to define this kind of breaks. Maybe someone could give me another hint?

Best wishes

Anja

messages.subject: Getting discrete colors on plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is my first post; I'm new to R but am a senior statistical programmer.  I have done a lot of graphs using SAS Graph but now am trying to transition to using graphs in R.

I'm trying to produce a graph where the colors have three categories- ideally I would like them to be Green for good, Yellow for Questionable, and Red for bad.

So I tried to do this in GGPLOT; here is my code:

id <-       c(1,2,3,4,5)
x1 <-       c(5,2,3,5,1)
x2 <-       c(4,1,3,5,1)
x3 <-       c(5,2,3,5,1)
x4 <-       c(4,3,3,5,1)
x5 <-       c(3,1,3,5,1)
colorvar <- c(3,1,2,3,1)

mydata <- data.frame(id,x1,x2,x3,x4,x5,colorvar)
head(mydata)

# convert to long format
require("reshape")
mydata_long <- melt(mydata, id=c("id", "colorvar"))
head(mydata_long)

require("ggplot2")
p <- ggplot(data=mydata_long,
       aes(x=variable, y=value,
group=id, colour = colorvar)) +
    geom_line()
p

This works, but I get more colors on the graph than my colorvar has.  I have 3 colors on my colorvar, but 5 colors show up on the graph, including 1.5 and 2.5.   How do I tell ggplot only to use the 3 colors and not give me a gradient of colors?  Also how would I specify the colors that I want, such as the RGB equivalents of green, yellow, and red?  My real data will have many more records.

-Mary

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mary, you tell R that 'colorvar' is a factor, not a continuous variable:

mydata_long$colorvar <- factor( mydata_long$colorvar )

For your second question, you add a manual color scale to your plot:

p+scale_color_manual(values=c("green","yellow","red"))

Regards,
Ben

For example, if you are calling a column in a data.frame in aes() you should only need to put Attribute and not label.data$Attribute. Does this work for you?

ggplot()+
geom_line(data = time.data
   , aes(
     x = as.numeric(Date2)
   , y = value
   , group = Attribute
   , color = Color)
   , size=1)+
geom_text(data = label.data
   , aes(
     x = Inf
   , y = value
   , label = Attribute
   , color = Color
   )
   , size=4
   , vjust=0
   , hjust=1
   )+
facet_grid(Attribute.Category~.,space="free")+
theme_bw()+
scale_x_continuous(
breaks=as.numeric(unique(time.data$Date2))
,labels=format(unique(time.data$Date2)
,format = "%b %Y"))+
theme(strip.background=element_blank(),
      strip.text.y=element_blank(),
      legend.text=element_blank(),
      legend.title=element_blank(),
      plot.margin=unit(c(1,5,1,1),"cm"),
      legend.position="none")+
 scale_colour_identity()

messages.body_plain:
One other possibility is lack of antialiasing: if you're generating the images on Windows or Linux, some or all of the elements will not be antialiased. One way to work around this is to use CairoPNG from the Cairo package to generate the images.

On a Mac, the default is to use the Quartz output device, which does properly antialias everything.

Regarding file size: the command-line program optipng will make your png files smaller, without changing the appearance.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Equation and R2 on graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi Oscar -

Here's another way of doing it, for linear models. Maybe you can find some ideas from it. In the code below, I show two methods: one with manually-created expressions, and another with expressions automatically generated from the lm object.

# Given a model, predict values of yvar from xvar
# This supports one predictor and one predicted variable
# xrange: If NULL, determine the x range from the model object. If a vector with
# two numbers, use those as the min and max of the prediction range.
# samples: Number of samples across the x range.
# ...: Further arguments to be passed to predict()
predictvals <- function(model, xvar, yvar, xrange=NULL, samples=100, ...) {
  # If xrange isn't passed in, determine xrange from the models.
  # Different ways of extracting the x range, depending on model type
  if (is.null(xrange)) {
    if (any(class(model) %in% c("lm", "glm")))
      xrange <- range(model$model[[xvar]])
    else if (any(class(model) %in% "loess"))
      xrange <- range(model$x)
  }
  newdata <- data.frame(x = seq(xrange[1], xrange[2], length.out = samples))
  names(newdata) <- xvar
  newdata[[yvar]] <- predict(model, newdata = newdata, ...)
  newdata
}

model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, mtcars)

# First generate prediction data
pred <- predictvals(model, "wt", "mpg")
sp <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg)) + geom_point() + geom_line(data=pred)

# === Plot with manual annotation ===
# Use x=Inf and y=Inf to place in corner, then use hjust and vjust to adjust
# position of text label inside plot area.
sp + annotate("text", label="r^2 == 0.75", parse = TRUE, x=Inf, y=Inf, hjust=1.2, vjust=1.5)

# =================================
# Auto-generate expression from model object
eqn <- as.character(as.expression(
  substitute(italic(y) == a + b * italic(x) * "," ~~ italic(r)^2 ~ "=" ~ r2,
    list(a = format(coef(model)[1], digits=3),
         b = format(coef(model)[2], digits=3),
         r2 = format(summary(model)$r.squared, digits=2)
))))
eqn
# "italic(y) == \"37.3\" + \"-5.34\" * italic(x) * \",\" ~ ~italic(r)^2 ~ \"=\" ~ \"0.75\""

# === Plot with generated expression ===
sp + annotate("text", label=eqn, parse=TRUE, x=Inf, y=Inf, hjust=1.1, vjust=1.5)

-Winston

On Fri, Jan 18, 2013 at 10:49 AM, Oscar Branson <ob...@cam.ac.uk> wrote:
> I often find that I want to place the equation of a line drawn with stat_smooth or geom_line on a ggplot graph.  As far as I can tell, there is no standard way to do this.  Granted, there is the problem that the fit functions are very variable, so it's hard to format the output correctly in all cases, but there must be some way around this...
>
> I am no expert at R coding, and have come up with a rather 'messy' solution, that combines fragments of strings together to produce a character string that can be parsed by ggplot's annotate command.  At the moment, it can deal with linera (y=mx+c) and polynomial (ns(x,order), from the splines package) functions.
>
> I realise that my solution is rather crude, but I am not aware of a better way of going about it.  Any thoughts/comments/suggestions would be very welcome!
>
> Thanks!
>
> ......Code follows......
>
> set.seed(1000)
>
> ts=data.frame(x=seq(0,10,0.2),y=seq(0,10,.2)^2-0.1*seq(0,10,.2)^3+rnorm(length(seq(0,10,.2)),0,0.4))
>
> # have a look at the data - I want to put the equation of the line, and the R2 value at the top of the graph.
> p=ggplot(ts) + geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y)) + stat_smooth(aes(x=x,y=y),method='lm',formula=y~ns(x,3))
> p
>
> # Equation for getting the coefficients and R2 values from a fit.  Parameters are
> # df = data frame
> # x.var = string denoting the x data in the df
> # y.var = string denoting the y data in the df
> # signif.figs = the number of significant figures you want the coefficients and R2 to.
> # eq.plot = T/F, whether to plot the equation, or just the R2.  F = just R2
> # model.type = 'lin' or 'poly', for the two types of model I have designed it for
> # order = if using 'poly', the order of the polynomial.
>
> lm_eqn = function(df,x.var,y.var,signif.figs,eq.plot=T,model.type,order){
>   if(missing(x.var) | missing(y.var) | class(x.var)!='character' | class(y.var)!='character') stop('x.var and y.var must be the names of the columns you want to use as x and y as a character string.' )
>   if(missing(model.type)) stop("model.type must be 'lin' (linear y~x model) or 'poly' (polynomial y~ns(x,order) model, generated by splines package).")
>   if(model.type=='poly' & missing(order)) stop("order must be specified if poly method is used.")
>
>   if(eq.plot==T) {
>     # Linear y=mx+c equation
>     if(model.type=='lin') {
>       fit = lm(df[[y.var]] ~ df[[x.var]]);
>       eq <- substitute(italic(y) == c + m %.% italic(x)*","~~italic(r)^2~"="~r2,
>                        list(c = signif(coef(fit)[1], signif.figs),
>                             m = signif(coef(fit)[2], signif.figs),
>                             r2 = signif(summary(fit)$r.squared, signif.figs)))
>       as.character(as.expression(eq));
>     }
>     # polynomial expression generated with the ns(x,order) function [splines package]
>     if(model.type=='poly') {
>       fit = lm(df[[y.var]] ~ ns(df[[x.var]],order));
>
>       base = gsub('!c!',signif(coef(fit)[1],signif.figs),"italic(y) == !c! + ")
>       element.1 = "!m! %.% italic(x)~"
>       element.2 = " + !m! %.% italic(x)^!o!~"
>       element.r2 = gsub('!r2!',signif(summary(fit)$r.squared,signif.figs),"~~italic(r)^2~\"=\"~!r2!")
>       eq=""
>
>       for(o in 1:(order)) {
>         if(o==1) {
>           if(coef(fit)[(o+1)]<0) tmp=gsub("[+]","",base) else tmp=base
>           eq=paste(tmp,gsub('!m!',signif(coef(fit)[(o+1)],signif.figs),element.1),sep="")
>         }
>         if(o>1) {
>           if(coef(fit)[(o+1)]<0) tmp=gsub("[+]","",element.2) else tmp=element.2
>           eq=paste(eq,gsub('!o!',o,gsub('!m!',signif(coef(fit)[(o+1)],signif.figs),tmp)),sep="")
>         }
>         if(o==(order)) eq=paste(eq,"\",\"",element.r2,sep="")
>       }
>     }
>   }
>   if(eq.plot==F) {
>     # Linear y=mx+c equations
>     if(model.type=='lin') {
>       fit = lm(df[[y.var]] ~ df[[x.var]]);
>       eq <- substitute(italic(r)^2~"="~r2,
>                        list(r2 = signif(summary(fit)$r.squared, signif.figs)))
>       as.character(as.expression(eq));
>     }
>     # polynomial expression generated with the ns() function [splines package]
>     if(model.type=='poly') {
>       fit = lm(df[[y.var]] ~ ns(df[[x.var]],order));
>
>       eq = gsub('!r2!',signif(summary(fit)$r.squared,signif.figs),"italic(r)^2~\"=\"~!r2!")
>     }
>   }
>   return(eq)
> }
>
> # To implement:
> eqn = annotate("text",x=5,y=16,label=lm_eqn(ts,'x','y',3,T,'poly',3),parse=T)
> p + eqn
>
>

messages.subject_clean: Possible to arrange plots in a grid using facet_grid... but facet in x and y with one variable?
messages.body_plain:
library(ggplot2)

## This makes a data frame that has groups "a" to "p"
## In this example the groups are different, but
## there are only two "classes":
##       1) random normal mu=30 and sigma = 10
##       2) random normal mu=0  and sigma =  1
## In real life each group could be unique, i.e.
## there is no systematic pattern in the real data..

df = data.frame(
loc=as.factor(rep(sample(letters[1:16]),each=10)),
a = c(rnorm(80, 30, 10), rnorm(80)),
b = runif(160,4,10))
df = df[order(df$loc),]

## Plot the data with each group in facet:
ggplot(df, aes(x=a,y=b,colour=a)) + geom_point() +
facet_grid(loc~.)
 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-yj_zkNljOmM/UPmfZKRbJhI/AAAAAAAABNI/4dYRokgHci8/s1600/ggplot+1.png>

## Now I was hoping to arrange them in a grid
## I make a "group" factor so that I could make facets 4 x 4
df$locGroup = as.factor(rep(1:4, each=40))
ggplot(df, aes(x=a,y=b,colour=a)) + geom_point() +
facet_grid(loc~locGroup)

## Can I collapse the blank parts of the graph and make a 4 x 4 plot?

messages.subject_clean: Possible to arrange plots in a grid using facet_grid... but facet in x and y with one variable?
messages.body_plain:
Gene,

I don't think this is possible. You have unique data for each "loc". There is no way for ggplot2 to know how to put "a" next to "e", "i" and "m". The only way I can think of is to subset your data logically (a-d, e-h, i-l, m-p), plot each graph independently and use grid.arrange() to put them next to each other. You would need to tweak these plots a lot:
remove the legends from each plot
give the legend it's own space (otherwise the final graph will have a different width)
remove ticks and extra space between plots to make it look like a facet
get rid of y-axis text on most plots
All possible, just depends how much you want your graph to look like what you want.

B

> df$locGroup = as.factor(rep(1:4, each=40))
> ggplot(df, aes(x=a,y=b,colour=a)) + geom_point() +
> facet_grid(loc~locGroup)

> <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-MLrUTa_BWmU/UPmfddrpbhI/AAAAAAAABNQ/SIfKoDBU0W8/s1600/ggplot+2.png>

Why not use facet_wrap?

ggplot(df, aes(x=a,y=b,colour=a)) + geom_point() +

facet_wrap(~loc, nrow=4, ncol=4)

Or if you want them columnwise, you can change the order of levels on
the faceting variable

df$loc2 <- factor(df$loc)
levels(df$loc2) <- as.vector(matrix(levels(df$loc2), 4, 4, byrow=TRUE))

ggplot(df, aes(x=a,y=b,colour=a)) + geom_point() +

facet_wrap(~loc2, nrow=4, ncol=4)

Or if the locGroup structure isn't that simple, you could create a new
variable which is the place-in-column for each locGroup

library("plyr")
df <- ddply(df, .(locGroup), mutate,
             col = as.numeric(factor(loc)))

ggplot(df, aes(x=a,y=b,colour=a)) + geom_point() +

facet_grid(locGroup~col)

--

Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Using position_dodge on point geoms
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 list members,

I have some data with identical (x,y) values. Is it possible to use
position_dodge() to avoid the points overlapping? I have tried to do
so, but only get strange warnings and results.

Example:

d=subset(iris, Petal.Length < 2)
sunflowerplot(d[, 3:4]) # The ‘petals’ indicate duplicate points

# Ordinary plotting hides these duplicates
ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) + geom_point(size=3)

# One solution is to use jittering, but even then some points
# may by chance happen to lie directly on top of each other
ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) +
   geom_jitter(size=3, position=position_jitter(w=.01,h=.01))

# So I want to use dodging. But just setting position="dodge"
# doesn’t work:
ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) +
   geom_point(size=3, position="dodge")

# Setting ‘width’ and ‘height’ only seems to have
# the effect of compressing the plot horizontally
# (only ‘width’ seems to matter – ‘height’ has no effect)
ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) + '
   geom_point(size=3, position=position_dodge(width=.1, height=.1))

I also get strange warning, ‘ymax not defined: adjusting position
using y instead’, but neither ‘position_dodge’ nor ‘geom_point’ takes
a ‘ymax’ argument, AFAICS.

And I don’t really understand the documentation at
http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3/position_dodge.html
Looking at plots 3–7, it seems like ‘position_dodge’
doesn’t have an effect at all?

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer

messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

See in line below.

On Sat, Jan 19, 2013 at 12:49 PM, Karl Ove Hufthammer
<Karl.Hu...@math.uib.no> wrote:
> Dear ggplot2 list members,
>
> I have some data with identical (x,y) values. Is it possible to use
> position_dodge() to avoid the points overlapping? I have tried to do so, but
> only get strange warnings and results.
>
> Example:
>
> d=subset(iris, Petal.Length < 2)
> sunflowerplot(d[, 3:4]) # The ‘petals’ indicate duplicate points
>
> # Ordinary plotting hides these duplicates
> ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) + geom_point(size=3)
>
> # One solution is to use jittering, but even then some points
> # may by chance happen to lie directly on top of each other
> ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) +
>   geom_jitter(size=3, position=position_jitter(w=.01,h=.01))
>
> # So I want to use dodging. But just setting position="dodge"
> # doesn’t work:
> ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) +
>   geom_point(size=3, position="dodge")
>
> # Setting ‘width’ and ‘height’ only seems to have
> # the effect of compressing the plot horizontally
> # (only ‘width’ seems to matter – ‘height’ has no effect)
> ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width)) +
>   geom_point(size=3, position=position_dodge(width=.1, height=.1))

position_dodge is for dodging groups. Since you have no groups defined
dodging has no effect. You can create groups as I've done below (note
that there is probably a better way to do this...)

tmp <- unique(d[c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")])
tmp$group <- interaction(tmp)
d <- merge(d, tmp)
d <- ddply(d, "group", transform, gn = factor(1:length(group)))

 Now you can dodge the groups

 ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width, group = gn)) +
   geom_point(size=3, position=position_dodge(width=.08))

Personally I don't like this approach very well. Jiiter works better
in my opinion. Or you could size by the number of points:

d <- ddply(d, "group", transform, gsize = length(gn))

 ggplot(d, aes(x=Petal.Length, y=Petal.Width, size = gsize)) +
   geom_point()

>
> I also get strange warning, ‘ymax not defined: adjusting position using y
> instead’, but neither ‘position_dodge’ nor ‘geom_point’ takes a ‘ymax’
> argument, AFAICS.

I see that a lot, and just ignore it.

>
> And I don’t really understand the documentation at
> http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3/position_dodge.html
> Looking at plots 3–7, it seems like ‘position_dodge’
> doesn’t have an effect at all?

I think that is a documentation error. There is no dodging there for
the same reason there was no dodging in your original effort. The
example should be set up as

df <- data.frame(x=c("a","a","b","b"), y=1:4, g = rep(1:2, 2))
(p <- qplot(x, y, data=df, group=g, position="dodge", geom="bar",
stat="identity"))

then the remaining examples should work.

Best,
Ista
